47353: Stephen and Philip, two of the Seven, soon become powerful preachers and evangelists. Service roles were not boxes.
47354: Good structure, chosen for character and recognised by the community, frees every kind of ministry and lets those closest to a need help meet it.
47356: What does Paul ask of a young church leader?
47357: Timothy has been left in Ephesus to correct false teaching. He is young, perhaps timid, and often unwell (1 Tim 4:12, 2 Tim 1:7, 1 Tim 5:23).
47359: His gift came through prophecy and the laying on of hands by Paul and the elders. Ministry is received and confirmed in community (1 Tim 4:14, 2 Tim 1:6).
47361: "Keep a close watch on yourself and on the teaching." Character and content go together (1 Tim 4:16).
47363: He is to entrust what he has heard to faithful people who can teach others, four generations of discipleship in one verse (2 Tim 2:2).
47365: Preach the word, be ready in season and out, correct, rebuke and encourage with patience, endure suffering and do the work of an evangelist.
47366: Christian leadership is a trust: received through community, guarded by character, centred on the word and multiplied by training others.
47368: What does the first Spirit-filled person in Scripture teach about ministry?
47369: God says, "I have called by name Bezalel." Call language is used for a craftsman, not a priest or prophet.
47371: He is filled with the Spirit of God, with ability, intelligence, knowledge and all craftsmanship. This is the first time Scripture says someone is filled with God's Spirit.
47373: Oholiab is given to work with him, and both are given the ability to teach others (Exod 35:34). Skilled women spin and give (Exod 35:25-26).
47375: Their work makes the tabernacle, the place where God dwells among his people. Art and craft serve worship and presence.
47376: Skill in making things can be a Spirit-given ministry. The church today should honour artists, builders and makers as servants of God.
47377: What does an elderly widow in the temple show about hidden ministry?
47379: Anna, daughter of Phanuel of the tribe of Asher, is called a prophetess. She was widowed after seven years of marriage and is now very old.
47381: She never left the temple, "worshipping with fasting and prayer night and day". Luke uses a verb (latreuō) often used for priestly service.
47383: Seeing the infant Jesus, she gives thanks and speaks about him to all who were waiting for the redemption of Jerusalem. She is among the first to proclaim Christ.
47385: Her life matches the enrolled widows of 1 Timothy 5:5, who continue in prayer night and day.
47386: Faithful prayer over many years is ministry, and God gives a hidden servant a central place in announcing the Messiah.
47387: What does "ministry" mean? Diakonia as service
47388:
The English word "ministry" comes from the Latin *ministerium*, "service". In the New Testament it usually translates the Greek *diakonia*, and a minister is a *diakonos*. These words cover a wide range. Martha's work in the kitchen is diakonia (Luke 10:40). The women who supported Jesus "served" him from their resources (Luke 8:3). The apostles' preaching is the "ministry of the word" (Acts 6:4), and Paul calls the whole gospel task "the ministry of reconciliation" (2 Cor 5:18). Even a collection of money for poor believers is a diakonia (Rom 15:25-27).

For a long time scholars assumed that diakonia meant humble, menial service, like waiting on tables. In 1990 the Australian Catholic scholar John N. Collins (*Diakonia: Re-interpreting the Ancient Sources*) argued that in Greek usage the words more often meant acting as a commissioned agent or go-between, carrying out a task on someone else's authority. Many scholars now accept that both ideas are present: a diakonos is someone sent and authorised, and the task may well be lowly. Jesus holds both together when he says he came "not to be served but to serve" (Mark 10:45).

Old Testament Hebrew has its own service words. The verb *'abad* (to work, serve, worship) describes Adam's work in the garden, Israel's worship of God and the Levites' tabernacle duties. The verb *sharat* is used of priests and Levites "ministering" before the LORD. In both testaments, then, ministry means doing God's work on God's behalf for the good of others. It is not first a job title but a way of life that some people also carry out in recognised roles.
47389: John N. Collins' work on diakonia sparked a debate. Some, including many Catholic and Anglican writers, think it shows diakonia was a commissioned, even official, role. Others, such as the German scholar Anni Hentschel, developed his approach further, while many still stress that care for the needy remains part of diakonia. The two readings are complementary rather than opposed.
47390: Israel's offices and what they were for
47391:
Israel's calling was first a corporate one: at Sinai the whole nation is called "a kingdom of priests and a holy nation" (Exod 19:6). Within that people God appointed particular servants. Priests from Aaron's family brought sacrifices, blessed the people and taught the law (Lev 10:10-11, Num 6:22-27). Levites guarded and served the sanctuary and later taught and sang (Num 8, 1 Chr 25). Prophets were called one by one to speak God's word, usually to confront power (Deut 18:15-22). Judges delivered tribes in crisis (Judg 2:16-19). Kings were to rule under the law, not above it (Deut 17:14-20). Elders represented families and settled disputes at the gate (Ruth 4:1-11). Scribes and sages taught and counselled (Jer 18:18).

These offices had a shared purpose: to keep Israel in covenant relationship with God and to make God's rule and presence real among the people. They also checked one another. Prophets anointed and rebuked kings (1 Sam 16:13, 2 Sam 12:1-14); kings could not take a priest's role (1 Sam 13:8-14, 2 Chr 26:16-21). Power was spread out.

The Old Testament is honest that every office failed. Priests like Eli's sons abused worshippers (1 Sam 2:12-17), prophets spoke lies for money (Mic 3:5-11), and kings led Israel into idolatry. Ezekiel 34 condemns Israel's "shepherds" for feeding themselves instead of the flock and promises that God himself will shepherd his people through a coming David. This hope prepares for the New Testament claim that Jesus fulfils these offices.

Service was not limited to formal offices. The Nazirite vow was open to men and women (Num 6:2). Bezalel, a craftsman, is the first person said to be filled with God's Spirit (Exod 31:3). Women served at the entrance of the tent of meeting (Exod 38:8). Ministry in Israel was broader than its offices.
47392: Jesus, the true Prophet, Priest and King
47393:
The New Testament presents Jesus as gathering up Israel's offices in himself. He is the prophet like Moses, whose words must be heard (Acts 3:22-23), and God's final word (Heb 1:1-2). He is the great high priest who offers himself once for all and now intercedes for his people (Heb 7:23-28). He is the Son of David, given all authority in heaven and on earth (Matt 28:18). Each title is now filled by "Christ", which means "anointed one", since prophets, priests and kings were all anointed.

The church historian Eusebius (early fourth century, *Church History* 1.3) already linked Christ with all three anointed offices. John Calvin developed it into the doctrine of the threefold office (*munus triplex*) in his *Institutes* (2.15). Catholic teaching adopted the same language at Vatican II, which says all the baptised share in Christ's priestly, prophetic and kingly office (*Lumen Gentium* 31). Orthodox, Lutheran and Reformed theologians also use it.

Two points matter for ministry. First, Jesus defines his offices by service. He is a king who washes feet (John 13:12-17) and a priest who is also the sacrifice. Any ministry that copies the world's way of "lording it over" others contradicts him (Mark 10:42-45). Second, because Christ has fulfilled these offices, Christian ministry does not repeat them but shares in his ministry. Traditions differ on how: Catholic and Orthodox churches see the ordained priest as acting in the person of Christ at the Eucharist; Protestant churches stress that Christ is the only mediator and all believers share his priesthood. Both agree no minister replaces Christ.
47394: The "threefold office" is a theological summary, not a phrase found in Scripture. It is widely used across Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant theology, and is a helpful lens rather than a test of orthodoxy.
47395: Apostles then and now: the debate
47396:
An apostle (*apostolos*) is "one sent" with authority. The New Testament uses the word in at least three ways. First, the Twelve, chosen by Jesus as witnesses of his whole ministry and symbol of renewed Israel (Mark 3:13-19, Acts 1:21-22). Second, Paul and a wider group who saw the risen Lord and were commissioned by him to found churches, such as Barnabas, James the Lord's brother and probably Andronicus and Junia (1 Cor 15:5-9, Acts 14:14, Rom 16:7). Third, "messengers" (apostoloi) sent by churches on a task, such as Epaphroditus (Phil 2:25, 2 Cor 8:23).

Are there apostles today? There are three main answers. (1) Most Protestant traditions, and most cessationists, say no in the foundational sense: the church is "built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets" (Eph 2:20), and a foundation is laid once. They point to the requirement of seeing the risen Christ (1 Cor 9:1) and Paul's description of himself as "last of all" (1 Cor 15:8). Apostolic authority now resides in the apostolic writings. (2) Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican churches teach apostolic succession: bishops succeed the apostles in teaching and governing, not as eyewitnesses but as guardians of the apostolic faith, as Irenaeus and Clement of Rome already argued. (3) Many Pentecostals and charismatics hold that apostolic ministry continues in a functional sense: pioneering missionaries and church-planters who lay foundations in new places. A smaller group, often called the New Apostolic Reformation, teaches that apostles hold governing authority over churches and networks today.

These views overlap more than they seem. Almost everyone agrees that the Twelve and Paul were unique, that the New Testament is the authoritative apostolic witness, and that the church must stay "apostolic" by holding to their teaching and continuing their mission. The real disagreement is whether any present-day person can bear the title with authority, and how that authority is checked.
47397: Ask anyone who claims apostolic authority the questions the New Testament asks: Is the message the apostolic gospel (Gal 1:8)? Is the person accountable and tested (Rev 2:2)? Does their life show the marks of an apostle, including suffering and servanthood (2 Cor 11:23-30)?
47399:
Ephesians 4:11 says that the ascended Christ "gave the apostles, the prophets, the evangelists, the shepherds and teachers, to equip the saints for the work of ministry, for building up the body of Christ". Since "shepherds and teachers" share a single article in Greek, many read them as one role, making four groups rather than five. The purpose clause is clear: these gifts exist to equip everyone else (Eph 4:12-16).

Cessationists (for example Richard Gaffin, Thomas Schreiner, and in a stronger form John MacArthur) argue that apostles and prophets were foundational gifts for the first generation (Eph 2:20, Eph 3:5). Evangelists, pastors and teachers continue. Prophecy in the sense of new revelation has ceased now that Scripture is complete. They value the stability and sufficiency of Scripture this gives, and warn against new claims of authority.

Continuationists (for example Wayne Grudem, Gordon Fee, Sam Storms, Craig Keener) argue that nothing in Ephesians 4 says some gifts will end before the church reaches maturity in Christ (Eph 4:13), and that New Testament prophecy was weighed and was not equal to Scripture (1 Cor 14:29, 1 Thess 5:19-21). Many of them accept ongoing prophecy and pioneering "apostolic" mission while rejecting new governing apostles. Alan Hirsch's APEST model, popular among missional churches, treats the five as functions every church needs, not ranked offices.

The New Apostolic Reformation (NAR), a label used by C. Peter Wagner from about 1996, teaches that God is restoring the offices of apostle and prophet to govern the church, with apostles over networks and prophets bringing fresh revelation for strategy. Supporters say this recovers biblical patterns and explains the rapid growth of independent networks worldwide. Critics, including many Pentecostals and charismatics as well as authors R. Douglas Geivett and Holly Pivec, warn that it can create unaccountable authority, encourage extra-biblical revelation and politicise prophecy. Some leaders associated with the label reject it as describing an organised movement.
47400: For the wider debate on whether miraculous gifts continue, see /debates/cessationism and /movements/prophetic-movement. Many continuationists reject the NAR's view of governing apostles; it is wrong to treat all charismatics as NAR.
47402:
Local churches in the New Testament were led by groups of elders (*presbyteroi*). Paul and Barnabas appointed elders "in every church" (Acts 14:23), and Paul addressed the Ephesian elders as those whom the Spirit had made overseers (*episkopoi*) to shepherd the flock (Acts 20:17, Acts 20:28). Titus 1:5-7 again uses "elder" and "overseer" for the same people. Most scholars therefore agree that in the New Testament period the two words describe one office: "elder" points to maturity and dignity, a term from Jewish life; "overseer" points to the task of supervision, a term from Greek civic life.

The qualifications in 1 Timothy 3:1-7 and Titus 1:5-9 are striking for what they emphasise. Only one is a skill, "able to teach". The rest concern character and relationships: faithful in marriage, self-controlled, hospitable, not violent or quarrelsome, not a lover of money, managing the household well, respected by outsiders. Elders lead by example, not domination (1 Pet 5:3).

Deacons (*diakonoi*) appear alongside overseers (Phil 1:1). Their qualifications are similar, without the requirement to teach, and they must "be tested first" (1 Tim 3:8-10). 1 Timothy 3:11 speaks of "women" (gynaikes), which could mean deacons' wives or women deacons. Many early church sources describe women deacons, especially in the East, who assisted at baptisms of women and visited women in their homes.

How churches apply this varies. Presbyterians distinguish teaching and ruling elders (from 1 Tim 5:17). Many Baptist churches have one pastor plus deacons, or a plural eldership (Alexander Strauch's *Biblical Eldership* argues strongly for the latter). Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican churches have bishops, priests and deacons, seeing the single bishop as a legitimate early development. Congregational churches stress the authority of the whole membership.
47403: Women in ministry: three main approaches
47404:
Scripture names many women who served God: Miriam the prophet who led Israel's song (Exod 15:20, Mic 6:4), Deborah the prophet and judge (Judg 4:4-5), Huldah, whom the king's officials consulted about the book of the law (2 Kgs 22:14-20), Anna the prophetess (Luke 2:36-38), the women who supported Jesus and were first witnesses of the resurrection (Luke 8:1-3, Luke 24:1-10), Priscilla, who taught Apollos with her husband (Acts 18:26), Phoebe the deacon and patron (Rom 16:1-2), Junia among the apostles (Rom 16:7), Euodia and Syntyche who "contended at my side" (Phil 4:2-3), and Philip's prophesying daughters (Acts 21:9). Paul assumes women pray and prophesy in worship (1 Cor 11:5).

The same letters contain passages that restrict women's roles: "women should keep silent in the churches" (1 Cor 14:34-35) and "I do not permit a woman to teach or to exercise authority over a man" (1 Tim 2:11-15). How to hold these together is the question.

Complementarians (John Piper, Wayne Grudem, Thomas Schreiner, Andreas Köstenberger, Kathy Keller) argue that 1 Timothy 2 grounds its instruction in creation (1 Tim 2:13), not culture, so it applies today; that elders are described as men (1 Tim 3:2); and that women's many ministries in Scripture never include elder oversight. Equal dignity is affirmed, but roles differ. Egalitarians (Gordon Fee, Philip Payne, Craig Keener, Lynn Cohick, Michael Bird) argue that Paul's practice shows women in leadership, that 1 Timothy 2 addresses a specific situation of false teaching in Ephesus, that the Greek *authentein* is a rare word that may mean domineering, that the creation reference may be illustration rather than universal rule, and that the trajectory of Galatians 3:28 and Acts 2:17-18 points toward full participation.

Catholic and Orthodox churches approach the question differently. They reserve the priesthood and episcopate to men mainly for sacramental reasons: Christ chose twelve men, and the priest represents Christ the bridegroom at the Eucharist (*Inter Insigniores*, 1976; *Ordinatio Sacerdotalis*, 1994). At the same time they honour women as saints, martyrs, abbesses, theologians and Doctors of the Church, such as Catherine of Siena and Teresa of Ávila, and Mary the mother of Jesus is honoured above all. Discussion continues about women deacons, which existed in the early church; Pope Francis opened the ministries of lector and acolyte to women in 2021, and the Patriarchate of Alexandria consecrated deaconesses in 2017.

All three camps include people who take Scripture with full seriousness. A fair conversation recognises that the disagreement is about how to read particular texts, not about whether women are equal before God (Gal 3:28, 1 Pet 3:7).
47405: Myth: "Complementarians think women are inferior" or "egalitarians ignore the Bible." Both are straw men. Leading complementarians affirm full equality of dignity, and leading egalitarians argue from careful exegesis of the same texts. See /debates/gender-roles.
47406: Ministry outside church walls: work as worship
47407:
Most Christians spend most of their waking hours outside church gatherings. Scripture treats that time as ministry too. Adam's first task was to "work and keep" the garden (Gen 2:15), using words that later describe priestly service; work was worship before the fall. Joseph ran a grain programme, Daniel served in government, Nehemiah was a cupbearer, Lydia traded in purple cloth and Paul made tents (Gen 41:46-49, Dan 6:3, Neh 1:11, Acts 16:14, Acts 18:3).

Paul tells even slaves to work "heartily, as for the Lord and not for men", because "you are serving the Lord Christ" (Col 3:23-24). He urges believers to work quietly with their hands so as to be respected by outsiders and not dependent (1 Thess 4:11-12), and to work in order to have something to share (Eph 4:28). Ordinary work, done well, honestly and for the good of others, is service to Christ.

The Reformers drew on this to reject the medieval idea that monks and priests had a higher "religious" vocation. Luther taught that a milkmaid or a shoemaker serves God in their calling. Modern writers such as Dorothy L. Sayers ("Why Work?", 1942), Miroslav Volf (*Work in the Spirit*, 1991), R. Paul Stevens (*The Other Six Days*, 1999) and Tim Keller (*Every Good Endeavor*, 2012) develop the theme. Catholic teaching, especially after Vatican II, stresses that lay people sanctify the world from within through their work and family life (*Apostolicam Actuositatem* 2).

This does not erase the importance of gathered church ministry or of supporting those who preach the gospel (1 Cor 9:14). It means the church gathers to be equipped, then scatters to serve.
47408: Try asking at the end of a work day: Whom did I serve today? What did I make or keep that God cares about? Where did I reflect his character?
47409: The clergy-laity divide and its history
47410:
The New Testament uses *laos* ("people") for the whole people of God and *klēros* ("lot" or "inheritance") for the whole people as God's portion (1 Pet 5:3, where elders are not to dominate "those in your charge", literally "the lots"). It has no separate word for a clergy class. Yet it does recognise leaders who are to be respected, supported and obeyed (1 Thess 5:12-13, 1 Tim 5:17-18, Heb 13:17).

By the early second century, Ignatius of Antioch describes a single bishop with presbyters and deacons. In the third century Cyprian of Carthage and others speak of a clergy order distinct from the laity, and Old Testament priestly language begins to be applied to Christian ministers. After Constantine, clergy received legal privileges. In the medieval West, clerical celibacy, Latin liturgy and the Gregorian reforms of the eleventh century widened the gap, and "religious" came to mean monks and nuns.

The Reformation challenged this. Luther taught that all the baptised are priests and that ordained ministers are servants appointed by the community for public preaching and sacraments. Anabaptists went further, stressing congregational discernment and mutual ministry. Later, Pietists, Methodists, Pentecostals and the house-church movement each pushed for wider lay participation. In the Catholic Church, Vatican II taught that clergy and laity share one dignity and mission, with lay people carrying the apostolate into the world (*Lumen Gentium* 30-38, *Apostolicam Actuositatem*).

Views of this history differ. Catholic and Orthodox writers see the ordained ministry as a genuine gift of the Spirit that grew from apostolic roots, while admitting clericalism (the abuse of clerical power) is a real danger; Pope Francis repeatedly criticised clericalism. Many Protestants see the clergy-laity divide as a departure from Scripture that the Reformation began to correct, while often recreating it in their own churches with a "pastor does everything" culture. A balanced view keeps both truths: God gives leaders, and every believer is a minister.
47411: The words "clergy" and "laity" come from Greek words that in the New Testament describe the whole church. The separation into two classes is a post-biblical development, judged differently by different traditions.
47412: Ministry in Jewish and Mediterranean terms: household, hospitality, patronage
